tools.name: find_people
tools.description: Count and sample people by job title, seniority, department, where they are, and who they work for or used to work for, including the employer's revenue, headcount, industry and location. Free: it changes nothing and spends nothing, so run it before asking how many people to save. Answers with the match count and at most five sample people. A place is where the PEOPLE are unless the person says it is the employer's ('at US companies' is company_countries). Send every wording of a title. Every other filter (skills, languages, schools, years in role, past employers, employer growth and funding) is a more_filters row. It cannot narrow by the technology an employer runs.

company_names.description: Company names to include, any of them, matched on the brand rather than the legal entity.

exclude_company_names.description: Companies to leave out: existing customers and competitors, never to narrow a search.

company_domains.description: Bare domains like stripe.com: the most exact way to name a company, so prefer them to names.

company_industries.description: Industries from the fixed list, e.g. Software Development; one outside it is refused naming the nearest.

company_headcount_min.description: Fewest employees to accept. Unset is no floor.

company_headcount_max.description: Most employees to accept. Unset is no ceiling.

company_revenue_min.description: Least annual revenue in US dollars (10000000), the current employer's on a people search. Many companies lack it, so it shrinks a search: say so rather than call a small number a small market.

company_revenue_max.description: Most annual company revenue, in US dollars.

keywords.description: Words in a headline or company description; loose, so only for an idea no other filter carries, never a title or industry.

job_titles.description: Job titles to include, as alternatives. Each also finds its spellings (& or and, SVP or Senior Vice President, Sr. or Senior); send a role's other wordings too: 'Head of IAM', 'Head of Identity and Access Management'. A list of titles is roles to find: search wide, sort who is found after.

tools.name: list_search_filters
tools.description: Read every filter one lead search takes, exactly as the Find leads page offers them: each filter's name, what it takes (words to include and exclude, a range, yes or no, a day, one choice) and what it means, with its choices spelled out. Which ones the search tool's own arguments set is marked; every other one is a more_filters row on that tool. Read it before telling anybody a search cannot narrow by something, and whenever a more_filters name or its choices are not clear. The same names are what get_search_behind_table prints and change_table_search_filters sets. Free, and it calls nothing.

search.description: Which search to read every filter of.

tools.name: list_tables
tools.description: List this workspace's tables with each one's row count, folder, owner, whether it is archived and, for a table of people or of companies, its table_type (a line with no table_type is an Other table), most recently changed first. Start here whenever a person refers to a table by name, because every other table tool needs the id this gives you; a search finds archived tables too, and matches the description as well as the name, as the page's search does. Scope picks the list: every table on the list, or all of them ordered by when this person last opened each, this person's favorites or the ones they opened recently, the archived ones, the untouched ones nobody in the workspace has opened or changed for a while (what to suggest archiving; nothing archives a table by itself), the ones waiting for a folder since folders replaced tags, or Trash with the folders in it. folder narrows it to the tables directly in one folder ('which tables are in Events'), and beside a scope, a search, or an owner to that folder and every folder under it, as the Tables list narrows within the folder open; owner narrows it to one person's ('my tables', 'the ones Maya owns'); table_type to one type ('my company tables', the tables a people search can follow with a company_table row). It reads no rows.

scope.description: all: newest change first; opened: their last opened first. starred, recent: their own Favorites and Recent. untouched: unused for months. unfiled: waiting for a folder. trash: deleted tables and folders (sequences: list_trashed_sequences). (default: 'all')

name_contains.description: Only tables with this in the name or description, any case. (default: '')

folder.description: A folder, its subfolders too beside a filter: name, path, id, top level. (default: '')

owner.description: One person's tables: name, email, me, no owner. (default: '')

limit.description: How many tables to list. 50 at most. (default: 25)

tools.name: get_table
tools.description: Read one table: its name, its description, how many rows it has, when it was created and last updated (a row added or a value written), its folder (top level when in none), its owner (No owner when none), whether it is archived, and every column with that column's type and whether it is typed in by hand, calculated, or filled in by a run; a select or multi_select column also lists its options, the only values its cells take, and a column that only runs on some rows says so: follows_view names the saved view it follows, has_run_condition marks a condition of its own. It also carries the table's settings (auto_run, keep_existing_results, share_shape_by_link, each on or off, and table_type: person, company or other, and whether its lead search set it), its column groups with their members, and its health: how many cells are currently errored, whether a run is going on right now, and whether the table has hit its row cap. Each column is one short line by default; name columns in columns, or set include_setup, to read them in full: an AI column's prompt, its outputs as name: type, its run condition, model, switches, group, display (hidden, pinned and width as the person asking sees them, the color the team's), what one row costs, the columns it reads and the columns that use it (what depends on this column). Read a column in full before changing it. This is what to read before answering anything about what a table holds, and before writing into a select. It returns no rows; use read_table_rows for those.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

columns.description: Columns to show in full (prompt, outputs, run rules, what uses them).

include_setup.description: Show every column in full. (default: False)

tools.name: read_table_rows
tools.description: Read a table's rows as values under the column names the person sees, filtered, sorted and searched in one call. where takes conditions on named columns, all of which hold unless a joiner says or, and a group number brackets some of them: 'SaaS or Fintech, and over 50 people' is the two industries in group 1 joined by or; sort orders the result; contains finds rows by text, in TEXT cells only, so compare numbers and dates with where instead. The matching count comes back whatever the page size is, which is how to answer 'how many rows have no email' without reading any. ids_only answers with row ids alone, ready to hand to edit_table_rows, delete_table_rows or rerun_table_rows. one_row_per keeps, of the rows the rest keeps, the first of each value of one column in table order: values match exactly, case included, and every row blank there stays, a cell of only spaces too. The default page is 20 rows and the most in one call is 100. A cell that is not a plain value comes back marked: [still running] or [waiting to run] while a run is still working on it, [nothing found] when it ran and came back empty, [failed], [not run], [cancelled before it ran], and [out of date] when its inputs changed after it ran, with the old value it still shows. A value the grid marks Low confidence ends in [low confidence] (an email at another company than the row's, say); explain_table_cell gives the reason. Count them apart: while cells are still running, answer like '3 of 5 done, still looking for 2', never 'none found'.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

column_names.description: The columns to read, by their exact names; empty reads the first 12. Name only those needed. Omitted fields are unknown, not empty. To judge a person's identity, include the full, first and last name fields there are; a blank combined name never justifies replacing a contact.

where.description: Only rows matching these, up to 8; empty for the whole table. (maxItems: 8)

one_row_per.description: A column, by name: only its first row per value (one per domain). Blanks stay. (default: '')

sort.description: Order by these columns, first key first, up to 3. Empty: the table's order. (maxItems: 3)

contains.description: Only rows with this text, any case, in TEXT cells: compare numbers, dates and checkboxes with where. (default: '')

ids_only.description: Only the matching row ids and count: for edit_table_rows, delete_table_rows or rerun_table_rows. (default: False)

limit.description: How many rows to read. 100 at most. (default: 20)

offset.description: Rows to skip from the top. (default: 0)

view.description: With show_on_page: the saved view on screen, by name or id, to lay this over unsaved. Empty: Default. (default: '')

RowFilterArg.description: One condition a row has to satisfy.

column.description: Column name or 'Column › Field'; 'any column' with has_error or has_no_error asks the whole row.

operator.description: has_error, has_results, has_not_run, is_stale and run_stopped ask what a cell's last run DID; has_error also finds a bad email or link. The rest: what it HOLDS.

value.description: Text, read as a number or true/false against such a column. Empty for operators taking none (is_empty, is_true, has_error and the run-state family). The _any_of ones: alternatives separated by commas, one holding a comma in double quotes; (empty) is blank cells. (default: '')

joiner.description: or: any condition at its level may hold; and: all. (default: 'and')

group.description: Conditions sharing 1, 2... are bracketed. (minimum: 0; maximum: 8; default: 0)

RowSortArg.description: One key a row listing is ordered by.

column.description: The column to order by, by name. Write 'added' to order by when the row was added, or 'edited' by when it last changed.

descending.description: Largest or newest first. Blank cells always sort last, either way. (default: False)

tools.name: create_table
tools.description: Create a table, empty or filled from CSV the person pasted into the chat. Never make one to stand in for a search that found nobody: say no one matches and offer to widen the filters. Given csv_text the first line is the column names, every column is text, up to 200 rows and 25 columns: a pasted list, not a file. For a file attached to a message use import_file_as_table, which takes any size and types each column; for one not attached, point them at Import from file on the Tables page. Free.

name.description: What to call it, in the person's words, 40 characters at most: detail goes in description. Unique in the workspace: a taken name is refused. Empty when they named none: New table, numbered when taken. (default: '')

description.description: One line on what the table is for. Leave empty for none. (default: '')

csv_text.description: CSV to fill the table with, first row being the column names. Comma separated, quotes around any value that contains a comma. Leave empty for an empty table. Paste what the person pasted. (default: '')

folder.description: The folder to make it in: name, path or id. A campaign's or a list's tables share one folder named for it; a name not there yet makes it. (default: '')

tools.name: edit_table_rows
tools.description: Add rows to a table and write or empty its cells, in one call. This is the ordinary grid edit: naming the column and the row, it writes the value a person would type. add_rows adds empty rows, at the bottom or above or below a row named by id, and set_cells can fill them in the same call by calling them new1, new2 and so on. It edits VALUES only: it cannot add, rename or retype a column, and it cannot write into a cell a formula or an enrichment owns. A select or multi_select cell takes only the column's own options, which get_table lists: a value that is not one is refused with the options named, and nothing in that call is written. Then say so, and offer to add the value to the column's options with update_table_column's add_choices, or to use an existing option. A decimal or currency value is rounded to the column's decimal places, and the answer names what was stored; report that, not what was sent. Editing a cell that a computed column reads makes that column stale, and running it again costs what it cost the first time. Free in itself. Set dry_run to check an edit and count its cells without writing anything.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

add_rows.description: Add this many empty rows first, at the bottom unless placed. Their ids come back in the answer; set_cells names them new1, new2 and so on. (minimum: 0; maximum: 1000; default: 0)

add_rows_above.description: Row id: new rows go above it. (default: '')

add_rows_below.description: Row id: new rows go below it. (default: '')

set_cells.description: The cells to write a value into. (maxItems: 1000)

clear_cells.description: The cells to empty, so the column's default shows again. A cleared value is gone: only a paid re-run of its column brings one back. (maxItems: 1000)

dry_run.description: True checks it and writes nothing. (default: False)

CellEditArg.description: One cell to write a value into.

row_id.description: The row's id, from read_table_rows, or new1, new2 and so on for a row this call adds.

column.description: The column's name, exactly as the table shows it.

value.description: The new value, as text: a number column stores a number, a checkbox true or false. A decimal or currency value is rounded to the column's decimal places, half away from zero; the answer names any value stored that way. A select or multi_select column takes only its own options (get_table lists them), matched ignoring case; separate multi_select options with commas. A value that is not an option is refused, so never write a near miss: offer to add it to the column's options first.

column.description: The column's name, exactly as the table shows it.

tools.name: update_table
tools.description: Rename a table or change the one line that says what it is for. Those two things only: turning runs on or off, changing what a rerun keeps and sharing the table's shape by link each cost money or give something away, and live on update_table_settings where the card says so, as does the table's type (Table type). Free.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

name.description: The new name. Leave empty to keep it. (default: '')

description.description: The new description. Empty keeps it. (default: '')

current_name.description: Its name now, for the approval card only. Not sent anywhere. (default: '')

tools.name: list_table_views
tools.description: List a table's saved views, with what each one filters on, how it sorts and which columns it hides, all in the person's own column names, which columns follow it, running only on its rows, and which sequences read their contacts through it. A view changes what the grid shows and never what the table holds; a filter saved on a view a sequence keeps in sync with applies to that sequence at once. Free.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

tools.name: list_table_runs
tools.description: Read a table's runs, newest first: what triggered each one, how far it got, how many cells failed, were held back by a run condition (skipped) or ran and found nothing (no data), and how it ended. This is what answers 'is it still running' and 'why did it fill only 40 of 50', and how an AI app follows a run it started, since nothing reports to one: look for the run its start named (its id, or the newest run when the start gave none), about a minute between looks. A running run that has not moved for a few minutes may be waiting to ask again for cells the AI model or a data source was too busy to answer, so do not call it stuck. Free.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

status.description: Only runs in this state: running, completed, completed_with_errors, cancelled, paused_for_credits or failed. Leave empty for all of them. (default: '')

limit.description: How many runs to read. 100 at most. (default: 20)

tools.name: stop_table_runs
tools.description: Stop what a table is running: one run by id, or every active run at once. Answers already in the table stay and are charged; a cell still working is dropped and costs nothing; the rest are left as they are and can be run again later. Nothing is deleted. Free, and it stops further spend. Set dry_run to see which runs would stop without stopping them.

table_id.description: The table's id, from a listing.

run_id.description: One run to stop, from list_table_runs. Leave empty to stop all of them. (default: '')

dry_run.description: True says which runs would stop and changes nothing: no card. Leave it false to stop them. (default: False)

tools.name: add_table_column
tools.description:
Add one column to a table. Four kinds, chosen with 'kind': a plain column people type into, of any type the grid has including select, multi select, list and object; an AI column that writes each cell from your prompt; an enrichment column that runs one catalog action on every row, such as find_work_email, verify_email or enrich_company, or one of the built-in agents; or a calculated column built from a plain sentence, with no formula syntax to write. REACH FOR A BUILT-IN AGENT BEFORE WRITING A PROMPT when one does the job: kind 'enrichment' with other_action_key use_case_match (the Use case finder: how the workspace's product would help each company, read from their site) or message_email (the Email writer: one subject and a first email with two follow ups kept in the table, built on a Use case column when the table has one). Asked for emails to the people in a table, build a draft sequence with build_sequence instead, and add the Email writer only when they still want the copy in the table after that. Both read the business context themselves. An AI column about the workspace's own product needs use_business_context on, never the pitch pasted into its prompt. AN AI COLUMN THAT ANSWERS SEVERAL THINGS DECLARES THEM AS outputs, each typed and each a column of its own (a Fit select with its choices, a Reason, a Contact name, a LinkedIn URL); never ask one cell for a labeled list, which nobody can sort, filter or build on. Fewer columns to pay for means one AI column with several outputs, not one answer holding everything. run_only_when keeps a column to the rows that pass a test on every run, which is how paid work waits for qualified rows; run_only_in_view keeps it to the rows of a saved view the person names, and follows that view as its filter changes. An AI column may also be given paid lookups, each charged only when it finds something: find_work_email and read_linkedin_profile. For 'who runs sales at each company' and the like, turn web_research on. Name other columns by their headers and they are resolved for you, including the columns an enrichment reads from, which are matched to its inputs by name. Adding an AI or enrichment column does NOT fill it in and spends nothing: run it with run_table_column, in the same reply, so the price is on one card. THE COLUMN IS ALREADY THERE once you have added it, even while that card waits, so say the column is on the table and approval fills it in: never that approving will add it, and never that the column is waiting for approval. Dismissing the card removes the column again. It will not change a column that already exists, and it adds one column at a time. Linked columns, the ways to fill one with prices before adding, or a cheaper way for one that exists: plan_table_columns. more_options takes the column editor's other settings as rows, option and value:
- run_delay_seconds (a whole number): Seconds to wait after its run condition is met before it runs.
- auto_run (yes or no): yes runs it by itself on new and changed rows while the table's own auto-run is on; left out, a column that spends credits on every row does not and every other one does.
- refresh_interval_hours (a whole number): Re-run it on its own this often, in hours. Spends credits every time.
- suppress_run (yes or no): yes saves a calculated column without computing it yet.
- use_row_context (yes or no): AI only: no reads only what the prompt names, not the whole row.
- starting_url_column_id (text): AI with web research: the Starting URL column, by name.
- stay_on_domain (yes or no): AI with a starting URL: yes keeps its research on that domain.
- json_schema (text): AI only: a strict JSON schema (an object) for its answer, instead of outputs.
- second_check (yes or no): Verify email: yes checks a catch-all again with a second verifier.
- after_column (text): Any kind: the column it goes right after, by name or id ('after this one': the open column). Last when not given.

table_id.description: The table to add the column to.

kind.description: plain: people type values; ai: prompt writes each cell; enrichment: one catalog action per row; formula: calculate from existing columns.

name.description: Unique header in the person's words. For built-in agents, name the whole answer ('Use case fit'); its fields get their own headers.

column_type.description: Plain only; other kinds infer their type. select/multi_select need choices; list holds same-type values; object holds a record. (default: 'text')

choices.description: For a plain 'select' or 'multi_select' column: the options people may pick, in the order to show them.

currency_code.description: For a plain 'currency' column: the ISO code, such as USD. Defaults to USD. (default: '')

decimal_places.description: Plain decimal/currency precision, default 2. All values are rounded to this many decimal places; retain enough for the source precision.

prompt.description: For kind 'ai' only, and required there: the column's goal in one to three lines, what to find and what a right answer gives. Name another column in double braces and this row's value is substituted: 'In one sentence, how would {{Company name}} use a GTM data platform, given {{Company › Description}}?'. The model cannot see the chat or any file, so put every fact it needs in the goal, the person's exclusions included, and never widen or relax them. Rules come from Needs work. The answer's shape is set by outputs. (default: '')

outputs.description: For kind 'ai': the separate answers each row gets, each saved typed. Declare one for every fact the person will sort, filter or act on. Two or more each get a column under this column's name; a lone output is the cell itself, so declare one only to type the answer. A row that holds several people or items needs a list for every attribute, aligned by position, or one list of complete records: a single-value output holds one. Leave empty for one text answer.

run_only_when.description: Non-plain: lasting row filter for every run; excluded rows cost nothing. Empty runs all. Same where grammar except has_/is_stale. Enforce the person's exclusions here, before any paid work: a rule written in the prompt still runs, and charges for, the row.

run_only_when_match.description: Whether a row must pass every run_only_when test or just one. (default: 'all')

run_only_in_view.description: Non-plain: run only in this saved view (name/id), following future filter changes. Use when the person names a view. Mutually exclusive with run_only_when. (default: '')

web_research.description: AI: search/read web pages (not PDFs/files), adding web-research cost from list_ai_model_tiers. Leave off for answers already in the row. (default: False)

find_work_email.description: AI: look up work email by name/company; charged only when found. Enable only when the task needs an address. (default: False)

read_linkedin_profile.description: AI: read LinkedIn headline, role and work history; charged only when a profile is returned. (default: False)

use_business_context.description: AI: enable for the workspace's product, fit, benefits or outbound messages. Supplies its business context; never paste the pitch into the prompt. (default: False)

ai_model.description: Effort level key, from list_ai_model_tiers (kind 'ai') or an agent's price. Leave empty for the default, which almost every column should use. (default: '')

action_key.description: Required for kind 'enrichment' unless other_action_key is given. One action returns many fields (enrich_company: size AND industry); add it once, not per output. The catalog lists outputs.

other_action_key.description: Enrichment key outside action_key; prefer a fitting built-in agent over a custom prompt. use_case_match finds how the workspace helps each company; message_email writes subject + three emails into the table using its Use case column. Offer build_sequence first for outreach; use message_email only if they still want table copy. Also icp_fit, company_research, person_research, or a key returned by list_enrichment_catalog (prefix optional). First three supply their own business context; output fields get separate columns. Leave empty when action_key covers it. (default: '')

input_columns.description: Enrichment input mappings. Empty matches columns by action input name; specify when that would select the wrong column.

instruction.description: Required for formula: calculation in plain words with column names, e.g. 'Extract the domain from Website'. No formula syntax needed. (default: '')

more_options.description: More settings, a row each: run_delay_seconds, auto_run, refresh_interval_hours, suppress_run, use_row_context, starting_url_column_id, stay_on_domain, json_schema, second_check, after_column. (maxItems: 20)

ColumnInput.description: One fact an enrichment needs, and the column that supplies it.

input.description: The canonical input name the action declares, exactly as list_enrichment_catalog printed it for the chosen action: names differ between actions. Not the name of your column.

column.description: The column holding that fact, or 'Column › Field'.

ColumnOptionRow.description: One setting of a new column given as a row: the shared row, described in fewer words.

value.description: Digits, yes or no, or text. (default: '')

ColumnOutput.description:
One answer an AI column returns per row.

Declare two or more and each gets a column of its own under the column's
name; a lone output is stored as the cell itself, since a column reading
it would be a copy of its parent.

name.description: Its header, in sentence case, for what IT holds rather than for the whole column: 'Fit', 'Contact name', 'LinkedIn URL'. No full stops.

holds.description: text, paragraph (a few sentences), url, email, number, decimal, checkbox, date, select or list. A verdict or tier from a fixed set, such as Strong, Possible or Poor, is a select with its choices. (default: 'text')

choices.description: For a select only, and required there: the answers it may give, in order.

description.description: What belongs in it when the name does not say, such as 'Not found unless a person can be verified'. Leave empty otherwise. (default: '')

RowCondition.description: One test a row must pass to be run.

column.description: The column to test, or 'Column › Field'. Empty with has_error or has_no_error tests every cell in the row at once. (default: '')

operator.description: eq, neq, contains, not_contains, starts_with, gt, gte, lt and lte take a value; is_empty, is_not_empty, is_true, is_false and the has_ ones none. has_ and is_stale only mean anything on a column something runs into.

value.description: What to compare against, as text; '1000' compares as a number. Empty for the operators that take no value. (default: '')

tools.name: run_table_column
tools.description: Fill in a column by running it over the table: every row, only the rows that are still empty, only the ones that failed, the first few, or the rows named in row_ids. Rows ticked on the page are row_ids: a run or a push to a connected tool asked for with rows ticked takes exactly them, as the table's Run and Export on ticked rows do, unless the person asks for all. A where filter narrows whichever scope you chose, in the same grammar as reading rows, for THIS run only; to hold a column back on every run, give it run_only_when instead. This is what spends credits, so set dry_run to price the work first: a dry run changes nothing, costs nothing, and answers with the rows in scope and the credits they would take. A real run starts the work and returns straight away; answers appear row by row afterwards, so never report values from it. It also fills in every column that reads this one, and the price covers them: a dry run answers with the most it can cost, what runs like it usually cost, and each column it fills. When a run started from the Chat finishes, the conversation gets a short report of what filled in, what came back with nothing and what failed; an AI app gets no report, and the answer gives it the run's id to follow with list_table_runs. A run that leaves out rows still empty in the column says how many, so offer to run those too. A column people type into cannot be run, and is refused before the card; so is a run the workspace's Anthropic key would stop (refused, out of credit or at its monthly limit), with the fix. To run several columns on chosen rows at once, use run_table_columns.

table_id.description: The table the column is on.

column.description: The column to run, by its name on the table. Its id also works.

scope.description: Which rows: 'all' every row; 'empty' cells with nothing yet, failed and stale included; 'failed' only failed ones; 'first_n' a sample off the top, to try a column first. (default: 'all')

limit.description: How many rows 'first_n' covers, 10 when left out.

where.description: Only rows passing these tests, narrowing the scope. Enforce the person's exclusions here or in the column's run_only_when; a rule in an AI prompt does not stop a paid run.

match.description: Whether a row must pass every test or just one of them. (default: 'all')

one_row_per.description: A column: only its first row per value runs. Blanks run. (default: '')

dry_run.description: Price the run instead, spending nothing: the rows in scope and their cost. Use it when asked a cost, and before a large run. (default: False)

row_ids.description: Only these rows, by id from read_table_rows or the ticks, not a scope. (maxItems: 1000)

RowCondition.description: One test a row must pass to be run.

column.description: The column to test, or 'Column › Field'. Empty with has_error or has_no_error tests every cell in the row at once. (default: '')

operator.description: eq, neq, contains, not_contains, starts_with, gt, gte, lt and lte take a value; is_empty, is_not_empty, is_true, is_false and the has_ ones none. has_ and is_stale only mean anything on a column something runs into.

value.description: What to compare against, as text; '1000' compares as a number. Empty for the operators that take no value. (default: '')

tools.name: list_enrichment_catalog
tools.description: List the enrichment actions a column can run on every row, what each one costs per row (one figure, or for an action whose sources are priced differently the most a row can cost and what one usually does, since a row is charged the price of the source that answered it), which columns it needs to read, and whether it can answer at all right now. Read it when somebody asks what can be found out about a list, or when the eleven keys named on add_table_column do not cover what was asked for. It does not say what a table already has, and it changes nothing.

search.description: Narrow the catalog to actions whose name, key or description matches these words: 'email', 'company', 'linkedin'. Leave empty to see everything, which is usually what you want the first time. (default: '')

tools.name: get_sequence
tools.description: Read one outreach sequence in full: whether it is a draft, running or paused, the table of people it writes to and how many that comes to (counted in the background after each change, so right after one it waits a few seconds for the fresh count and otherwise says the numbers shown are being updated; a launch always enrols from the table as it is), the senders it sends from and how much they can still send today, who has to approve what, its outbound agent (its Effort, whether it researches people and whether Draft replies is on, for which labels), every step numbered with its wait, either its words or, where the agent writes it, the prompt it writes from, and where it goes next when that is not the step below (a condition's Yes and No, a connection request's Connected and Not accepted and how long it waits for an answer, a jump, an early finish), what one contact costs to walk it at the agent's real prices, while it runs how many contacts are still starting and how many of its tasks wait for approval (the answer to 'has the launch started?'), and EVERYTHING STILL BLOCKING A LAUNCH. That last part is the answer to 'why can't I launch this', so there is no separate pre-flight tool to call. With no sequence named it lists every sequence instead, with status, contact counts and reply rate, which is the right first call when nobody has said which one; scope lists the person's own favorites ('starred') or the ones they opened lately ('recent') instead, as the Sequences list's presets do. Name a sequence by id or by the name on screen. It costs nothing, changes nothing and writes no message; how the agent writes is read and changed with the outbound agent tools.

sequence.description: By id or name. EMPTY lists them all with status, contact counts and reply rate: the first call when none is named. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

scope.description: Listing only: 'starred' is the person's favorites, 'recent' what they opened lately. (default: 'all')

tools.name: list_sequences
tools.description: List the sequences as the Sequences list shows them: its preset (All, the person's own Favorites, Recent), its Status and Sender filters, a folder, and its search, each with status, contact counts, reply rate, senders, folder, and id. 'Only the paused ones', 'which sequences send from Ana', 'what is in the Q4 folder'. With show_on_page the Sequences list moves to it: send only what changes, and remove_from_page clears scope, status, sender, folder, or search. get_sequence reads one in full; list_trashed_sequences lists Trash. Free, and it changes nothing.

scope.description: The list's preset: 'all' (the default), 'starred' (the person's own Favorites) or 'recent' (the ones they opened lately). (default: 'all')

status.description: Only sequences in this status, as the Status filter. None: every status.

sender.description: Only sequences sending from this sender, by name or id, as the Sender filter. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

folder.description: Only sequences in this folder (name, path Events / 2026, or id), under a filter or search its subfolders too; or top level for those in none. (maxLength: 600; default: '')

search.description: Only sequences whose name holds this, any case, as the list's search. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

tools.name: build_sequence
tools.description: Build a whole outreach sequence in one go: its name, the table of people it writes to (it sends weekdays 9 to 5 in each sender's timezone; timezone is for a sender with none), the senders it sends from, and its emails in order with the wait before each one. This is the answer when somebody asks for emails or follow ups for the people in a table: build the draft on that table rather than adding writer columns, which are only for copy they still want kept in the table after being offered this. With no steps it starts on three emails the agent writes, or on the Introduce your company template (campaign introduce_company), whose messages end on the business context's free offer, or ask for a short call when it has none. When they said how the emails should read ('keep them simple') or what each one should get the reader to do ('book a call'), leave steps empty and pass their words as voice and goal: the voice is added to every prompt the agent writes from and the goal is set on the agent as the sequence is built, on this one card, so never follow it with an update_outbound_agent card for the same wish; writer rows set its Effort and research the same way ('research each person first, use the deep model': model_key deep, person_research yes). record_ids builds it for just the rows the person picked. The three emails are ones its outbound agent writes for each contact, the day they are enrolled, 3 days later and 4 days after that. Given steps, they replace that cadence whole. Given template, it starts from a saved sequence template instead (list_sequence_templates lists them), as Use a saved template does on the Sequences page: every step (its wait, its branches, and its words or its prompt), a copy of the agent's settings (its goal, Effort, research and replies), and the sending window, sending priority, Unsubscribe footer, plain text setting, Keep in sync with the table, approvals and opportunity values come with it, a timezone given is not used, and it takes no steps or campaign; the table and senders given are the new sequence's own, and its launch check says what the template's steps still need. Each email is either written by the agent for each contact as they reach it, from a prompt you give it, priced per message by the agent's Effort, or written by you with {{Column name}} variables from the audience table. The agent writes the first email's subject for each contact, and a later email with no subject of its own is saved as a reply to the one before it. It leaves the sequence a DRAFT and sends NOTHING: launch_sequence is a separate step the person asks for after they have read it, edit_sequence_steps is how any other LinkedIn steps and condition branches are added because this tool builds emails and a template's own steps only, and the outbound agent tools are how the agent's goal, Effort and research are set. Read the audience table's columns first so the variables you write match real columns; one that matches nothing stays as literal text and blocks the launch. For email steps, check that the audience table has an email column; when it has none, say so above this card, in the same reply as the call, and offer work-email enrichment. For a LinkedIn-only draft, build the draft then use edit_sequence_steps to REPLACE all default emails with the requested LinkedIn steps and branches; do not require email enrichment or a mailbox. Recheck the audience after replacing the steps because reachability depends on the channels used. Ask which sender only when there is a real choice: the only sender there is gets added without being named, and senders stays empty when none exists. A mailbox that is warming up or has no sends left today is never a reason not to build the draft, because capacity only applies when emails send: build it and say when it can start sending. When the person names the steps, give each its name in their words; otherwise leave names out. Building is free; the answer says what sending will cost the contacts it can reach, which the person is told. Once it is built on a table, call write_sequence_previews in the same reply to write and show every contact's messages, free.

name.description: What to call the sequence. It cannot be a name already in use. (maxLength: 255)

timezone.description: An IANA timezone, such as Europe/Berlin, for a sender with none: the hours follow each sender's own. Leave it empty to take it from its senders, and with template, which keeps its own. (maxLength: 64; default: '')

table_id.description: The table of people it writes to, by id; rows with a usable address are enrolled, email and LinkedIn columns found for you. None named: ask the person which first (ask_question in Oneprofile's chat), or later. Empty means later; it cannot launch then. A table of companies, not people, is refused: find_people with a company_table row naming it finds their people. (default: '')

view_id.description: A saved view on that table, by id, to write to its rows only. Leave it empty for the whole table. Its sort is the order contacts go out in. (default: '')

record_ids.description: Only these rows of the table, by row id. (maxItems: 1000)

writer.description: Its agent's model_key, research and person_research, one row each. (maxItems: 3)

senders.description: The senders to send from, each by the name on screen or by id. When the workspace has exactly one, it is assigned for you, so leave this empty. Leave it empty to choose senders later; a sequence cannot launch without at least one, but its draft never waits for one. (maxItems: 100)

steps.description: The emails, in the order they go out, first to last. Leave it EMPTY to keep the cadence every new sequence starts with: three emails the agent writes for each contact, the day they are enrolled, 3 days later and 4 days after that, each from a default prompt. Give steps only to replace that cadence; what you give replaces it whole and is never added to it. (maxItems: 20)

campaign.description: none: three emails the agent writes. introduce_company: Introduce your company. Not with steps. (default: 'none')

channel.description: For a template: email, linkedin (profile view, request with no note, two messages if accepted), or both (email first). (default: 'email')

voice.description: How the person wants the emails to read, in their own words: 'keep them simple'. It is added to the prompt of every step the agent writes, as the sequence is built. Say how to sound, never what to say. Leave empty when they said nothing about it. (maxLength: 600; default: '')

goal.description: What every email asks the reader to do, in one sentence, when the person said: 'book a 20 minute call', 'get them to try the free plan'. Leave empty when they said nothing about it. (maxLength: 1000; default: '')

template.description: A saved sequence template to start from, by its name exactly as saved or its id. Its steps, prompts, agent settings and sending window come with it, so give no timezone, steps or campaign. Not an email template. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

template_name.description: The template's name, so the card names the template rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

OptionRow.description: One setting given as a row: which option, and its value in words or digits.

option.description: The option's name, exactly as the option list prints it.

value.description: Its value: a number as digits, yes or no, one of the option's choices, or text. A list is written with commas between its items. (default: '')

SequenceStepArgs.description: One email in a sequence, who writes it, and the wait before it goes out.

name.description: Its card's name, only when the person named the steps ('first email, first follow-up'): their words. Else leave empty. (maxLength: 80; default: '')

written_by.description: Who writes this email. 'agent' has the sequence's outbound agent write it fresh for each contact as they reach it, from the prompt below, their row and the workspace's business context. 'you' sends the subject and body given here to everyone. Left unset, a prompt means the agent and a body means you. (default: 'you')

subject.description: The subject line. Leave it empty on a follow up and it is saved as a reply to the email before it, in the same thread, which is what most follow ups should do. Leave it empty on the first email the agent writes, too: the agent then writes its subject for each contact. A first email you write yourself needs one. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

body.description: The email itself, as plain text with blank lines between paragraphs. Write a variable as {{Column name}} using the audience table's own column names, plus {{Greeting}}, {{Sender first name}} and {{Sending domain}}. {{Greeting}} already expands to 'Hi Ada' or 'Hi there': use '{{Greeting}},' alone, never 'Hi {{Greeting}}'. A name that matches no column stays as literal text and stops a launch, so use the column names you read from the table. Leave it empty when the agent writes this email. (default: '')

prompt.description: When the agent writes this email: what it should write, such as 'reference what their company does and ask for 15 minutes'. It is the brief for one message, never the words: the agent writes each contact's email from it. Give a body or a prompt, never both. (maxLength: 4000; default: '')

wait_days.description: Days to wait before this email, counted from the step before it. 0 on the first email sends as soon as somebody is enrolled. (minimum: 0; maximum: 365; default: 0)

tools.name: launch_sequence
tools.description: Launch a sequence so it starts sending. REAL EMAILS GO TO REAL PEOPLE from this point on, so only ever launch when the person has asked for it in so many words. Each email costs 0.1 credits as it goes out, every message the agent writes costs its Effort level's price on top (get_sequence says what one contact comes to, and the approval card prices the whole launch), a LinkedIn step costs 0.1 to 0.3 an action, and a Browser use step up to 56 credits a contact, 7 credits for each minute it runs, 8 minutes at most. A message the agent writes goes out on its own or waits for a person according to the strictest send mode among the sequence's senders, unless the sequence asks for every email to be approved. A LinkedIn step runs in its sender's paired browser, one at a time at that sender's Time between steps, and waits in Tasks for a person first unless the sender runs LinkedIn automatically and the sequence asks for no approval. The contacts due now start within seconds and the answer says how many, or, when the sending window is closed, when the roster starts. A launch that is not ready is refused with the reasons and nothing is sent; get_sequence lists those same reasons beforehand. A launch always asks a person, whatever the workspace has allowed. Set dry_run to check whether it would launch and who would start without launching or sending anything. Launching a sequence the setup wizard built also researches more of its people (their work email and Why them line), up to the number its setup said the credits cover, about 7 credits a person, from the workspace's balance: get_sequence's launch check says the total beforehand (its wizard_research_rest advice), and the answer says it again.

sequence_name.description: The sequence's name, so the approval card names it rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

dry_run.description: True checks the launch and says who would start, and changes nothing: no card, nothing sent. Leave it false to launch. (default: False)

tools.name: pause_sequence
tools.description: Pause a running sequence. Nothing of it is sent while it is paused: scheduling stops at once, its emails wait, and its queued LinkedIn steps leave every browser's line, approved or not. Only a LinkedIn step a browser was already handed may finish, and an email already handed to a mailbox may still go out. An approval given while it is paused is kept, and that step runs after Resume sequence; a held LinkedIn step can still be cancelled with decide_linkedin_steps, or its contact stopped with change_contact_journeys. A Browser use run whose cloud browser is open stops within seconds, and the minutes it ran are charged; the result says how many. Every contact stays exactly where it is, keeping its step, so resuming picks each of them up rather than starting anybody again. It does not remove anybody, does not change the steps, and is what to reach for before rebinding an audience, which a running sequence refuses. Set dry_run to check whether it would pause without pausing it.

sequence_name.description: The sequence's name, so the approval card names it rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

dry_run.description: True checks the pause and says what it would hold, and changes nothing: no card. Leave it false to pause. (default: False)

tools.name: resume_sequence
tools.description: Start a paused sequence sending again. Every contact picks up at the step it stopped on and nothing restarts at step one, so nobody receives an email twice. The contacts already due start again within seconds inside the sending window, and the LinkedIn steps it held go back in their senders' lines with every approval given while it was paused, at 0.1 credits an email, 0.1 to 0.3 credits a LinkedIn step and up to 56 credits a contact, 7 credits for each minute it runs, 8 minutes at most for a Browser use step, plus the agent's price for every message it writes, which is why this reaches people outside the workspace and asks first. It does not undo an individual contact's stop; change_contact_journeys does that. Set dry_run to check whether it would resume without resuming it or sending anything.

sequence_name.description: The sequence's name, so the approval card names it rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

dry_run.description: True checks the resume and says what would start again, and changes nothing: no card, nothing sent. Leave it false to resume. (default: False)

tools.name: edit_sequence_steps
tools.description: Add, edit, reorder or explicitly remove sequence steps, including LinkedIn and branches. Read get_sequence first. This tool takes the full list: include EVERY existing step with keeps_step, its number in that read, unless the person asked to remove or replace it. Omission deletes a step (a contact standing on it goes on to what follows it), so never omit one merely because it is outside the requested edit. Whatever you leave out of a kept step stays as it is, where it goes next included: a condition's Yes and No and a step's next keep the routing get_sequence prints in brackets unless you set if_yes_step, if_no_step or go_to_step, or finish_after_step, finish_if_yes or finish_if_no to end the sequence for a contact there. A connection request leaves by its answer, printed as 'connected (yes)' and 'not accepted (no)': if_yes_step or finish_if_yes is where Connected goes, if_no_step or finish_if_no where Not accepted goes, once it has waited condition_window_days for an answer (14 unless set), and both may go to the same step; go_to_step and finish_after_step are refused on it. A new request's Connected goes on down the list and its Not accepted gets a Withdraw, then finishes, which the card shows; finish_if_no or if_no_step leaves that out, and a kept request never gains one. already_connected own_branch gives contacts already connected to the sender their own branch (Connected is then called Accepted), going to if_already_connected_step or ending; with_connected folds it back. A withdraw a connected contact could reach is refused. An older Connection request accepted? check is kept with condition keep; taking it out hands its Yes to the request's Connected and its No to Not accepted. reply_to_step threads an email onto an earlier one. To change only prompts, use edit_message_prompts: this tool refuses a rewrite that only changes prompts. A call carrying a prompt always asks; a complaint about how the agent's messages read is mark_needs_work. A Browser use step is only kept, moved, renamed or removed here: set_browser_use_step changes one. Which kinds the agent may write, and what a LinkedIn step needs, are in kind and written_by. It sends nothing itself; a running sequence reads the new steps within a minute and contacts already past a kept step do not walk it again. A contact already waiting on a step whose wait changes waits the new time from when its wait began, so a shorter wait on a running sequence brings its next step forward, and that always asks a person; so does a shorter answer window, which sends contacts waiting on a request down Not accepted sooner. The card shows every change; a rewrite that changes nothing is refused. Name every step you add with name, in the person's words ('Customer example', 'Break-up'), never another step's name: a new email left unnamed is called for its place (Email 4), refused where that reads as another step on its path; name on a kept step renames it. When the person asks for steps 'at the end', 'after the last email' or anywhere that could mean more than one place, and the cadence splits (a condition or a connection request), ask the person where before calling this (ask_question in Oneprofile's chat), one option per place saying where and who gets the steps ('Right after Email 3 · everyone who hasn't replied, before the LinkedIn steps'), unless they named the step the new ones follow or the cadence runs in one line.

steps.description: The WHOLE cadence, in order, first to last. It replaces every step the sequence has: send it back with your edits in it, each step you keep marked with keeps_step. Steps asked for 'at the end' of a cadence that splits: ask the person which branch first (ask_question in Oneprofile's chat), unless they named the step the new ones follow. (maxItems: 20)

sequence_name.description: The sequence's name, so the approval card names it rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

EditStepArgs.description: One step of a cadence, of any kind the product has.

name.description: The step's name, in the person's words or for what it says: 'Customer example', 'Break-up'. Leave it out on a kept step to keep its name. Never a name another step already has. (maxLength: 80; default: '')

kind.description: What this step does. 'email' sends an email. The linkedin_ kinds hand the action to the sender's own browser and need a LinkedIn URL column on the audience table. 'linkedin_withdraw_invitation' takes back a connection request, so one must come before it on every path, under the request's Not accepted. 'condition' asks a yes or no question and splits the cadence in two. 'keep' leaves a kept step the kind it is, and makes a new step an email. (default: 'keep')

keeps_step.description: When this is a step the sequence already has: its number as get_sequence printed it. The step keeps its identity, so contacts standing on it stay there, and a step the agent writes keeps its whole prompt and what the agent has learned for it. Whatever you leave null, empty or 'keep' on a kept step stays as it is, where it goes next included. Give only what changes. Leave it unset for a new step. Each step the sequence has can be kept once.

written_by.description: Who writes this step's words. 'agent' has the sequence's outbound agent write them for each contact as they reach it, from prompt; it works on an email, a connection request's note, a LinkedIn message and an InMail, and on no other kind. 'you' sends the subject and body given here. 'keep' reads a prompt as the agent's and a body as yours, and leaves a kept step with whoever writes it now for as long as it still carries words. On a kept step the agent writes, 'you' with no body keeps the agent too: give the body you want sent to take the step over. 'no_note' sends a request with no note, the default to suggest: past a hidden LinkedIn cap, notes fail. (default: 'keep')

subject.description: An email's subject line, or a LinkedIn InMail's. Leave it empty on a follow up email and it is saved as a reply to the email before it, in the same thread. Leave it empty on the first email the agent writes, too, and on an InMail it writes: the agent writes those subjects for each contact. On a kept step, empty keeps the subject it has. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

body.description: The words this step sends: the email body, the LinkedIn message, or the note on a connection request. Variables are written {{Column name}} from the audience table, and a rotation is written {this|or this}, one phrasing chosen per contact. {{Greeting}} already includes 'Hi'; never prepend another greeting. Leave it empty on a step the agent writes and on one that carries no words. On a kept step, empty keeps the words it has. (default: '')

prompt.description: On a step the agent writes: what it should write there, as the brief for one message rather than the words themselves. Give a body or a prompt, never both. On a kept step, empty keeps the prompt it has. (maxLength: 4000; default: '')

wait_days.description: Days to wait before this step, counted from the step before it. Unset on a kept step keeps the wait it has; unset on a new step sends it straight after the one before, as no_wait does.

wait_hours.description: Hours to wait before this step, for a gap shorter than a day. Set this or wait_days, not both.

no_wait.description: True sends this step straight after the one before it, with no wait. Takes a kept step's wait away; never send it with wait_days or wait_hours. (default: False)

condition.description: On a condition step only, and required on a new one: what is being asked. 'bounced' needs an email step above it on every path that reaches it, or the graph is refused. Whether a request was accepted is its own branches, never a condition, and there is no reply check: a reply stops the sequence. 'keep' leaves a kept condition asking what it asks; one the sequence already has without it is let stand, and still blocks the launch until it is fixed. (default: 'keep')

condition_window_days.description: On a condition step: how many days back it looks. An Email bounced? check always decides within a day, whatever this says. On a connection request: the days it waits for an answer before Not accepted, 14 unless set. Unset keeps a kept step's.

if_yes_step.description: On a condition step: which step number a Yes goes to, and on a connection request where Connected goes, counting from 1 in the order you listed them. Unset on a kept step keeps the step it goes to now, wherever you list it, walking any new steps listed straight after it first; unset on a new one means the next step down the list. finish_if_yes finishes the contact instead.

if_no_step.description: On a condition step: which step number a No goes to, and on a connection request where Not accepted goes. Unset on a kept step keeps the step it goes to now, wherever you list it; unset on a new condition finishes the contact, and on a new request adds a Withdraw, then finishes. finish_if_no finishes it instead.

go_to_step.description: On a step that is neither a condition nor a connection request: which step number follows it. Unset on a kept step keeps the step it goes to now, wherever you list it, walking any new steps listed straight after it first, and the last of those goes on where it went; unset on a new one means the next step down the list. A step may only point FORWARD: pointing back would loop. finish_after_step finishes the contact instead.

finish_after_step.description: On a step that is neither a condition nor a connection request: True finishes the contact once it has run. Never with go_to_step. (default: False)

finish_if_yes.description: True finishes the contact on a condition's Yes, or a connection request's Connected. Never with if_yes_step. (default: False)

finish_if_no.description: True finishes the contact on a condition's No, or a connection request's Not accepted, with no Withdraw. Never with if_no_step. (default: False)

already_connected.description: On a connection request: 'own_branch' gives contacts already connected to the sender a branch of their own, Already connected; 'with_connected' sends them down Connected, the default. 'keep' leaves it. (default: 'keep')

if_already_connected_step.description: With own_branch: which step number Already connected goes to. Unset keeps a kept branch's and ends a new one.

reply_to_step.description: On an email: the step number, in this list, of an earlier email this one goes out as a reply to, in that email's thread (Re: its subject). Only for a thread other than the one just before it: an email with no subject already replies to the nearest email above it. Unset on a kept step keeps the thread it is in.

needs_approval.description: Hold this step for a person to approve even when its channel would run on its own. One way: it can add an approval, never remove one the sender or the sequence already demands. On a kept step, false keeps the hold it has. (default: False)

save_to_table.description: Profile view only: 'on' saves what it reads into the sequence's LinkedIn profile column, 0.1 credit per profile; 'off' does not. Unset: a new view saves, a kept one keeps its own. (default: 'keep')

annotations.title: Set or rewrite a sequence's steps

tools.name: add_contacts_to_sequence
tools.description: Add rows of a table to a sequence by row id. The rows must be in the sequence's own audience table; rows from anywhere else are refused, except that a draft with no audience yet takes the added rows as its audience. Rows already in it, rows with no email address, rows on Do not contact and rows over the limit of contacts per company are skipped, and the count says how many really joined. Added to a DRAFT they wait; added to a RUNNING sequence these people start getting emails within a minute, which is why that case asks a person. Set dry_run to count who would join without adding anybody.

table_id.description: The table the rows are in. It has to be the sequence's own audience table, unless the sequence is a draft with no audience yet, which takes the added rows as its audience (never a table that lists companies, not people); rows from anywhere else cannot be added.

record_ids.description: The rows to add, by row id, up to 1000 at a time. (minItems: 1; maxItems: 1000)

dry_run.description: True counts the rows the sequence would take and adds nobody: no card, nothing sent. Leave it false to add. (default: False)

tools.name: find_missing_emails
tools.description: Look up work emails for the contacts in a sequence's audience that have none, so its email steps can reach them. It covers only the audience rows with no address that a work email lookup has not tried yet, the same contacts the launch check lists as 'Find work emails for N contacts', and never a row that already has one. It spends credits per contact, so it always asks and the card quotes the price; to quote it in a reply first, read the estimate_missing_emails endpoint. When the audience table has no Work email column it adds one, bound to the name and company columns; when the sequence's email column already is one, found addresses land in it; otherwise a Default if empty column reads the email column first and the found email second, and the sequence switches to it once it has filled in. Emails arrive row by row over the next minutes. It does not verify addresses or launch anything.

sequence_name.description: The sequence's name, so the approval card names it rather than an id. Not sent anywhere. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

tools.name: get_outreach_analytics
tools.description: Read the whole workspace's outreach numbers over all time, the last week or the last month: contacted, sent, replied, positive (a person's label, or the agent's where the contact clearly showed interest), bounced, opted out, said no (a reply turning the offer down without asking to stop, never an opt out), and how many have had only the opener. It also reads the sender leaderboard, worst performer first: each MAILBOX's contacted, sent, replies and reply rate, positive replies, opt outs, said no and bounces, and each LinkedIn sender's connection requests, acceptances, messages and replies. That is how a deliverability problem is traced to one inbox, and which sender has the worst reply rate is read off it. There is deliberately no open rate and no click rate anywhere: these are plain text emails and there is nothing in them to instrument, so never report one. For one sequence, use get_sequence_performance; sequence_id here reads the analytics page's view scoped to one sequence, with the workspace's leaderboard.

period.description: Over all time, the last week or the last month. (default: 'all')

since.description: The first day to count, as YYYY-MM-DD. Set since, until or both for any other window, such as the last two weeks; period is then ignored. (default: '')

until.description: The last day to count, as YYYY-MM-DD, that day included. Empty is up to now. (default: '')

without_senders.description: True leaves out the sender leaderboard, which is read by default: each mailbox's sent, replies, reply rate, positive replies, opt outs and bounces, which is how a deliverability problem is traced to one inbox. (default: False)

sequence_id.description: Only one sequence's numbers, as the analytics page shows them scoped to it. Empty for the whole workspace. (maxLength: 64; default: '')

tools.name: get_sequence_performance
tools.description: Read one sequence's funnel: its contacted, replied, positive (a person's label, or the agent's where the contact clearly showed interest), bounced, opted out and said no numbers over all time, a week or a month; where every contact currently stands; each step's own sent, replies and bounces over all time, which is what says WHICH email is working, each step named as the Builder names it ('Step 2 · Email 2'; call a step by that name, never by an email's subject); on a step under an A/B test, each version's sent, positive, replied and bounced and the verdict in the panel's words ('Version B is winning', 'Too early to tell'), a winner judged on positive replies; how many are waiting at a step right now and how each condition split its contacts, and each connection request by branch and why, with how many still wait for an answer; and where the audience table keeps every email and LinkedIn message it sent, its '<sequence>: messages' column, one list per contact. There is no separate sent emails table any more. No open rate and no click rate exist here either. It costs nothing and changes nothing. Counts are not reply evidence: before diagnosing reply quality or copy, read_inbox for this sequence and read_conversation for representative exchanges now. If none came back, inspect sent messages and say no replies were available.

period.description: Over all time, the last week or the last month. (default: 'all')

since.description: The first day to count, as YYYY-MM-DD. Set since, until or both for any other window, such as the last two weeks; period is then ignored. (default: '')

until.description: The last day to count, as YYYY-MM-DD, that day included. Empty is up to now. (default: '')

tools.name: read_sequence_steps
tools.description: Read a sequence's steps whole: each step's words with their line breaks, its full subject and, on a step the agent writes, its full prompt, exactly as edit_sequence_steps and edit_message_prompts take them ({{Column name}} variables and {this|or this} rotations included), beside its name, kind, wait, who writes it, its approval and where it goes next. get_sequence prints every step short, on one line, and marks a field it cut [cut: N characters in all] or flattened [line breaks not shown] or [spacing not shown]: read those steps here before changing their words, subject or prompt, because what an edit sends replaces the whole field and words rebuilt from the short read lose what it left out. A preview shows one contact's message with the variables filled in, so it is never the words to send back. Name steps by their number in get_sequence's list or their step id, or leave steps empty for every step; a long sequence comes back as many whole steps as fit, naming the rest for another call. It costs nothing and changes nothing.

sequence.description: The sequence, by id or by the name on screen, as get_sequence takes it. (minLength: 1; maxLength: 255)

steps.description: The steps to read whole, each by its number in get_sequence's list (1 is the first), by its step id, or as 'message 2' for the message number get_sequence prints beside it; one step may be given alone. Leave it empty to read every step. (maxItems: 100)

tools.name: search_help
tools.description: Look up how something in Oneprofile works, and where in the product it is done. Reach for it whenever somebody asks how, where or why, and always before telling anyone the product cannot do something: a thing you cannot do for them is not a dead end if you can name the screen they do it on. It returns up to three help pages with a summary, a link to the documentation and the place in the dashboard. It reads the documentation only, so it tells you nothing about what is actually in this workspace and nothing about live prices.

question.description: What the person wants to know, in their own words: 'how do credits work', 'connect my mailbox', 'why are my rows not filling in'. Full questions work better than single words, because the search reads every word.

tools.name: get_pricing
tools.description: Read what things cost, in credits, from the product itself rather than from a written page: this workspace's credit balance (with how many of its credits expire at the next refill, and when, which answers 'do my credits expire' for this workspace), the headline price of finding a work email or a phone number or sending a message, the per row price of every enrichment action (the most a row can cost and what one usually costs, where a row is charged the price of the source that answered it), or what a lead search and its enrichments cost per row. Use it before quoting any price, because a price you remember is a price that has changed. It never quotes plan prices, invoices or amounts of money: the dashboard is the only place those are stated.

topic.description: Which prices to read. 'credits' for the workspace's balance and the headline price of finding an email, finding a phone number, verifying an address and sending a message. 'enrichments' for the per row price of each enrichment action a column can run. 'lead_search' for what a lead search costs per row, with the enrichments offered at import.

search.description: Only with topic 'enrichments': narrow the list to actions whose name or description contains these words, such as 'email' or 'company'. Leave empty for the whole catalog. (default: '')

record_type.description: Only with topic 'lead_search': which kind of search is being priced. Rows of different kinds cost different amounts. (default: 'people')

row_count.description: Only with topic 'lead_search': how many rows the person is thinking of adding, to quote a total beside the per row price. Leave unset for the per row price alone.

signal_type.description: Only with topic 'lead_search' on a signal search: the signal's key, so enrichments its own columns already cover are left out. (maxLength: 64; default: '')

tools.name: list_connected_sources
tools.description: List the tools this workspace has connected whose records can feed a table, and the kinds of record each one offers. Start here for anything about importing from a CRM or another system: every other import tool needs a name or an id from this list. It cannot connect anything, because connecting is a sign in a person does in Settings, under Connections. Free, and it changes nothing.

tools.name: preview_connected_records
tools.description: Sample a connected tool's records and report what is in them: the fields they carry with an example value each, which identifier rows would be matched on across refreshes and every other identifier they could be matched on (with why one would or would not work), whether the tool can say what changed since last time, and which fields an import would give their own columns. NOTHING IS CREATED: no table, no column, no row. Use it before proposing an import so the fields on the proposal are real ones. Free.

integration.description: The connected tool, named as the person named the connection, or its id from list_connected_sources.

record_type.description: Which kind of record, such as contacts or companies, spelled as the connection lists it.

tools.name: create_table_from_connected_tool
tools.description: Create a table fed by a tool this workspace has already connected, and start pulling its records in. Each record lands whole in one column, with the fields you name given their own columns beside it, and any other field can be given its own column later without re-fetching anything. Rows are matched across refreshes on the recommended identifier unless match_on names another the preview lists. The rows arrive in the background rather than by the time this returns, so do not read the table straight away. Importing spends no credits: the records are the customer's own. Called with no integration named it simply lists what is connected and changes nothing, so that call needs nobody's approval. It cannot connect a tool, and it cannot feed a table that already exists: that is a different table.

integration.description: The connected tool to import from, named as the person named the connection, or its id. Leave empty to be told what is connected; that call reads and changes nothing. (default: '')

record_type.description: Which kind of record to import, spelled as the connection lists it. Leave empty to be told what the chosen tool offers. (default: '')

table_name.description: What to call the new table, in the person's own words. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

row_limit.description: Most rows each refresh may pull. 0 pulls everything, which is what a table meant to mirror the tool wants. A limited source can never delete rows whose records are gone, because it cannot tell one it chose not to fetch from one that no longer exists. (minimum: 0; default: 0)

fields.description: Fields to give their own column, as the dotted paths preview_connected_records reports. Leave empty for the fields the preview suggests. Every field stays reachable later either way: the whole record lands in one column and promote_source_field_to_column can pull any path out of it without re-fetching anything.

match_on.description: Which identifier rows are matched on across refreshes, one of the fields preview_connected_records lists as matchable, for example email instead of the tool's own record id. Leave empty for the recommended one, which is what a person who did not ask wants. A field people can edit in the tool brings an edited record back as a new row. (maxLength: 255; default: '')

annotations.title: Create a table from a connected tool

tools.name: export_table_to_csv
tools.description: Read a small table out as CSV text, so it can be quoted back or handed over in the conversation: all of it, the rows a filter picks in an order ('only the Won rows, by revenue'), or rows by id. This is TEXT, not a download: a file, CSV or Excel, is saved only from the product's Export: Export above the table's grid or on ticked rows in it, or on the Tables page a table's row menu or Export with tables ticked (several download as one zip). More than 500 rows are refused rather than read out, because a whole table in a reply helps nobody; a filter that picks fewer is read out. Name the columns you want; every column of a wide table is almost never what was meant. It pushes NOTHING to a connected tool: sending rows to HubSpot or another CRM is add_export_column and then run_table_column. Free, and it changes nothing.

table_id.description: The table to export, from list_tables.

column_names.description: The columns to export, in this order, named exactly as the table names them. Leave empty for every column, which is usually far more than anybody wanted to read.

where.description: Export only the rows that meet every one of these conditions, each a column by its name, an operator and a value, as read_table_rows takes them: 'only the Won rows'. Leave empty for every row. (maxItems: 20)

one_row_per.description: A column, by name: of the rows where keeps, only the first of each value in it, as read_table_rows takes it. Blank rows stay in. (default: '')

sort.description: Order the rows by these columns, the first key first, as read_table_rows takes them. Leave empty for the table's own order. (maxItems: 3)

row_ids.description: Export exactly these rows, by the row ids read_table_rows prints, for 'these 20 rows'. Not together with where, one_row_per or sort. (maxItems: 500)

RowFilterArg.description: One condition a row has to satisfy.

column.description: Column name or 'Column › Field'; 'any column' with has_error or has_no_error asks the whole row.

operator.description: has_error, has_results, has_not_run, is_stale and run_stopped ask what a cell's last run DID; has_error also finds a bad email or link. The rest: what it HOLDS.

value.description: Text, read as a number or true/false against such a column. Empty for operators taking none (is_empty, is_true, has_error and the run-state family). The _any_of ones: alternatives separated by commas, one holding a comma in double quotes; (empty) is blank cells. (default: '')

joiner.description: or: any condition at its level may hold; and: all. (default: 'and')

group.description: Conditions sharing 1, 2... are bracketed. (minimum: 0; maximum: 8; default: 0)

RowSortArg.description: One key a row listing is ordered by.

column.description: The column to order by, by name. Write 'added' to order by when the row was added, or 'edited' by when it last changed.

descending.description: Largest or newest first. Blank cells always sort last, either way. (default: False)

tools.name: list_export_destinations
tools.description: List the connected tools a table's rows can be pushed to, with the objects each one takes and whether it can create, update or both. Name one of them and a record type to be told the fields a row can be matched on, which is what an export column needs. A destination that cannot match says so, and that matters: without matching, running an export twice makes two records. Free.

integration.description: One connected destination, by name or id, to be told exactly what it can do with a given record type. Leave empty to list every destination. (default: '')

record_type.description: The destination object, such as contacts or deals. Needed alongside integration to get the match fields an export column can use. (default: '')

tools.name: add_export_column
tools.description:
Add a column that pushes each row into a connected tool as a record. The cells hold the RECEIPT of each push, never the row's own data. Say how a row is matched to a record over there and what to write, as 'destination field=Column name' pairs read off list_export_destinations and the table's own columns. NOTHING IS SENT by adding it: an export column is created switched off and writes nothing until somebody runs it, which is why this is not a send. So when somebody asks for rows to be pushed or synced, this is only the first of two calls: call run_table_column on the new column in the same reply, or the person is left with a column and no records. With rows ticked on the page, that run takes exactly them as row_ids unless the person asked for every row.
